vignette:
Samir, a 40-year-old software engineer living with his wife in a suburban apartment complex, had always thought of himself as a steady, practical person-someone who solved problems by thinking them through. That changed one late autumn evening when a moderate earthquake, far stronger than anything the region had experienced in decades, struck without warning. He had been at his desk, writing code, when the floor began to shudder and the walls groaned. For twenty seconds that felt like hours, the building swayed, ceiling tiles fell, and glass shattered from a framed photograph on his desk. What stayed with him most vividly, even now, was the sound: a low, grinding roar from the earth beneath the foundation, mixed with the high-pitched screech of twisting metal and the panicked shouts of his neighbor in the next apartment. He could not later say in what order these things happened-the memory came as a jumble of images and sensations that he could never assemble into a clear timeline. When a memory surfaced, it arrived not as a recollection but as a full reliving: he would feel the tremor in his legs, smell the dust and ozone, hear the screech again, and his heart would race as if the ground were still moving.

In the weeks after the earthquake, Samir found himself unable to let the memory settle. At first he tried to force himself to think only positive thoughts-the building had held, he was alive, his wife was safe-but the command felt hollow, and the intrusive images broke through within minutes. He also noticed a growing, bitter obsession. The earthquake had been a natural disaster, but in his mind it had an author: the property management company that had neglected structural upgrades, the city inspectors who had signed off. He spent hours ruminating about how to get even with those he held responsible, drafting imaginary legal complaints and dwelling on vengeance scenarios even as he knew it made no sense. The anger gave him a strange energy, but it also kept the event fresh.

Samir's environment became laced with triggers. At the office, if a colleague approached his cubicle unexpectedly, he would flinch, his hands shooting up defensively. When someone tapped his shoulder to get his attention, he would whirl around, heart pounding, before he could identify the person. He began to map every room he entered for escape routes-where the exits were, whether a door opened inward or outward, whether the windows could be forced. He did this unconsciously now. His work as a software engineer required long hours in an open-plan office, but he had started choosing a desk against the wall, facing the door, and could not concentrate unless he had a clear path to the stairwell.

The negative appraisals took root quietly. He would think, Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation-he should have checked the building's seismic rating, should have moved to a safer area. Then the thought would spiral: Nothing good can happen to me anymore. Before the earthquake, Samir had been an easygoing, optimistic man. Now, he told himself he used to be happy but was always miserable. His wife noticed the change; he was irritable, withdrawn, and refused to go near the hospital where they had gone for treatment of minor cuts from the debris. When she suggested a routine physical, he snapped, "I don't need a doctor." He had come to believe that any medical setting-the sounds of gurneys, the antiseptic smell, the sight of an ambulance-would throw him back into the terror. He rerouted his drive home to avoid the medical center.

Months passed. Samir's avoidance narrowed his life. He stopped attending the weekly team outings his colleagues organized, afraid of the crowded, unfamiliar restaurants where he could not quickly find an exit. His wife grew distant, hurt by his refusal to talk about the earthquake and his sharp reactions to her touch. It was only when she told him, gently but firmly, that she could not keep living like this that he agreed to come for help. What frightened Samir most was the possibility that talking about the earthquake would break something inside him permanently-that the memories would overwhelm him and he would never put the pieces back in order. But he also hoped, with a small, tired part of himself, that somewhere in that conversation he might find the sequence he had lost, and a way to feel safe in his own skin again.
